decision_brief.authoring_note: Written from scratch for the 2026-10-01 snapshot after the full fresh recollection (see evidence/recollection/), including the newly captured Sep 30 BEA releases; no sentence is carried over from the 2026-09-30 brief.
decision_brief.headline: September 30 answered the frame's open question with firm numbers: GDP was revised up 0.7pp to 2.2% and core PCE still runs at 3.0% y/y, so growth is not cracking even as inflation stays sticky — and both boards still sit just above policy with no verifiable meeting distribution. Friday's September payrolls is now the single scheduled swing factor before the October decisions.
decision_brief.summary: Both central banks remain on hold — Fed 3.75-4.00% into Oct 27-28, BoC 2.25% into Oct 28 — and nothing verifiable is dislocated against policy: ZQV26, the October 30-day Fed funds contract, closed 96.110 on Sep 30 (unchanged across the session), implying a 3.890% October monthly (30-day) average EFFR, 1.5 bp above the 3.875% range midpoint; CRAU26's quote side (mid 97.63625; first executed print at 97.6375) implies roughly 2.364% quarterly average CORRA, about 11.4 bp above target. Neither is a meeting probability and CME FedWatch returned HTTP 403 again, so no single-meeting distribution exists anywhere in this snapshot. The new information since yesterday is in the data, not the prices: Q2 GDP's third estimate was revised up 0.7pp to 2.2%, August nominal PCE rose 0.9% with core PCE at 0.2% m/m / 3.0% y/y (new weight-0.5 hawkish card), and the tape says the same thing — the long end was sold again (TLT -0.58% on the day, -3.33% on the week) while equities slipped modestly (SPY -0.21%, ZEB -1.37%). The rates are patient; the data says patience is still the right read.

The contract averages almost the whole month before the Oct 28 decision, so it measures October's starting regime, not the meeting's outcome — it is an average contract, not meeting odds.

Core PCE proving sticky at 3.0% y/y in the September print (BEA schedule: Oct 29, alongside the Q3 GDP advance estimate) keeps cuts off the table; a core at 0.1% m/m instead revives the dovish tail.

Friday's payrolls is the week's cheapest way to get hurt: the October average sits at 3.890% (1.5 bp over the midpoint) and the long end has already been selling (TLT -3.33% w); a hot print compounds both.

Today's tape carries claims, ISM and a dense Fed-speak slate (Waller, Jefferson, Bowman, Cook, Williams) before Friday's print — headline risk without a verifiable meeting distribution to hedge against.
The BoC hawkish column is still empty by absence, not by evidence: a strong September LFS or an upward retail revision removes the dovish lean with no new BoC communication.
This frame expires at Oct 9 (LFS + Michigan) and definitively at the Oct 27-28/Oct 28 decisions; the missing direct pricing becomes a view on the data itself.

fed.rationale: The Sep 16 FOMC raised the target range 25 bp to 3.75-4.00%; that completed action is not itself an October surprise. FedWatch returned HTTP 403 again, so no single-meeting distribution exists in this snapshot and none is estimated. ZQV26 closed 96.110 on Sep 30 (unchanged across the session), implying a 3.890% October monthly (30-day) average EFFR — 1.5 bp above the 3.875% midpoint — but its average is set almost entirely before the Oct 28 decision, so it prices the pre-decision regime, not the meeting. The Sep 30 releases cut the other way from yesterday's dovish JOLTS: GDP was revised up 0.7pp to 2.2% and core PCE still runs at 3.0% y/y, so the new hawkish card (weight 0.5) balances the cooling evidence.

Neither board has a verifiable single-meeting distribution (FedWatch 403 again) and the verifiable contracts sit just off policy — the October Fed average 1.5 bp above the range midpoint, CORRA futures about 11.4 bp above target — so there is no dislocated price to trade against. The asymmetry worth watching now runs both ways: yesterday's cooling (JOLTS -256k) against September 30's firm data (GDP revised up; core PCE 3.0% y/y), with Friday's payrolls the first real adjudicator.
